subtopic: MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT SHELL CONTRACT-REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT SHELL CONTRACT-REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having given the notice required under the rules of the house, I wish to move, seconded by Mr. Rowe (Athabaska):
That a copy of the agreement between the government and the Montreal Construction Supply and Equipment Limited, Montreal,

War Munitions-Mr. MacNeil.
Quebec, for the machining of billets and forgings in the manufacture of shells, together with all related orders in council, documents, correspondence, minutes of the interdepartmental committee, and statements of claim, be referred to the standing committee on public accounts.
I consider it my duty very briefly to explain my reasons for requesting the reference to the standing committee on public accounts. I desire to make it very clear that I am actuated only by the conviction, which I hold very strongly, that the manufacture of armaments, or at least the primary implements of warfare, should be manufactured under national auspices. It is also my earnest desire to eliminate all forms of profiteering in the manufacture of armaments. I have had abundant evidence in recent weeks that this desire is shared by a large number of exservice men across the Dominion of Canada.
The reasons for suggesting that the house should refer this contract to the committee are found in the form and substance of the contract itself, which has been tabled in the house. It presents features very similar to those of the Bren machine gun contract, which necessitated a judicial inquiry, and which were found objectionable by many hon. members in this House of Commons.
The contract was placed by the government with the Montreal Construction Supply and Equipment Limited, Montreal, the president of which company is Mr. A. Janin. The contract was executed on November 17, 1937, and is for the machining of billets and forgings in connection with the manufacture of 20,000 quick-firing 18-pounder shell bodies, and 10,000 quick-firing 4-S-inch howitzer shell bodies. Although this contract was approved, I notice, by the interdepartmental committee, it was awarded on the basis of selection and not on the basis of competitive bids. I refer to the answer given by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) as it appears at page 627 of Hansard for February 3, 1939. According to that answer, this is the only contract which has been placed for the manufacture of shells in Canada, in Great Britain or any other country. In his answer the minister indicates that deliveries have not yet been made.
I believe the onus rests upon the government to explain fully, either in the house or before the public accounts committee, just what was involved in the negotiations leading up to the execution of this contract. I would remind the house that the government of Canada was committed at Geneva to a policy of the public manufacture of armaments, and on former occasions the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of National Defence assured the house they would

endeavour to follow such a policy. They also stated that the next best alternative would be manufacture on the basis of competition, under a suitable regulation of profits.
I ask the government to explain, either now or before the committee, why in the giving of this contract there has been such a marked deviation from a policy enunciated in the house and accepted by hon. members in good faith. I ask that, and propose that the committee should examine why the contract was awarded to this particular company.
I find, on reference to a directory issued by the Engineering Institute of Canada, that it is not listed as one of the companies in possession of facilities for the manufacture of products of this kind. Other companies are listed, and it is made abundantly clear that they have such facilities. I refer, at random, to companies included in the directory-five, for instance, named by the interdepartmental committee, with reference to the Bren gun, and companies such as Canadian Vickers, Limited; Montreal Locomotive Works, Limited; Ingersoll-Rand Company, Limited; Allis Chalmers Company; Dominion Engineering Works, Limited; Canadian Locomotive Company; Canadian Car and Foundry Company, Limited, and many others. These companies are established and actually in possession of the machine shop facilities required for the manufacturing or machining of the billets and forgings used in the manufacture of shell bodies.
I say that the committee should scrutinize closely the reasons why this construction company, a company interested mainly in the construction of buildings, with a machine shop which I understand is used chiefly for the overhauling of equipment used in construction, should be selected for this contract.
I think the committee should find out to what extent the public interests were safeguarded when the responsibility was assumed by the department or by the interdepartmental committee for the selection in this way of a favoured contractor. The committee should examine carefully the terms of the contract itself.
Under the provisions of the contract the government, the party of the first part, has undertaken to supply free of charge to this company, Montreal Construction Supply and Equipment Limited, all billets cut to length, forgings, base plates and driving band rings, special paint and varnish, and packages and boxes required for the said shells. These are all provided without charge. I believe the onus rests upon the government to explain to the committee or to the house from what source the billets and forgings will be ob-

War Munitions-Mr. MacNeil.
tained and if in that connection other contracts have been awarded. If other contracts have been awarded, we should be told upon what basis.
In another clause of the contract provision is made whereby the government shall supply such machinery as is set out in exhibit B of the contract, together with any additional machinery as may in the opinion of the said party of the first part be considered desirable. Referring to exhibit B, I find listed therein the type of machinery that one would expect to find in any well-equipped machine shop, and particularly the shops of those companies to which I have referred. There are listed heavy duty turning lathes, heavy duty boring lathes, ordinary lathes, rivetting machines, production drills, shaping and milling machines, universal tool and cutter grinder, and so on. Such machines are in common use in all well equipped machine shops. The question immediately arises: If the government already had any such equipment, why was it not used for government manufacture in connection with this order?
I believe there will be a responsibility upon the committee to examine closely the cost clauses of this contract, particularly in view of the answer given by the minister on February 3. At that time he said:
The contract was placed on a cost-plus basis at an upset manufacturing cost of $4 per shell for 20,000 shells, quick-firing, 18-pdr. high explosive, and $6.75 for 10,000 shells quickfiring, 4-5" Howitzer high explosive.
Clause 4 of the contract states:
The price to be paid by the party of the first part for the machining of the said billets and forgings shall be as follows:
(a)	The cost of electric current necessary for proper and healthy lighting of the shop, offices, corridors, lavatories, men's rooms and yard, which is hereby fixed in the sum of $1,270 per annum, commencing March 15th, 1938.
(b)	The cost of providing comfortable heat in cold weather, which is hereby fixed in the sum of $1,067 per annum, commencing March 15th, 1938.
(c)	The proportionate amount of all taxes, business, real estate and special, other than income tax, which amount is hereby fixed in the sum of $900 per annum, commencing March 15th, 1938.
(d)	The cost of the water supply in shop, yard, offices, men's rooms and lavatories, which is hereby fixed in the amount of $100 per annum, commencing March 15th, 1938.
(e)	The cost of maintenance and repair of railway siding, hereby fixed in the amount of $300 per annum, commencing March 15th, 1938.
(f) The cost of power supplied from the machine shop of the party of the second part for the ammunition ship compressor, in the maximum of 50 h.p., fixed in an amount at $1,500 per annum, the party of the first part hereby agreeing that any power in excess of
that herein mentioned which may be required shall be paid by it on a meter basis, commencing March 15th, 1938.
(g)	. The cost of four telephone connections and signal system from office to shop, fixed in an amount of $360 per annum, commencing March 15th, 1938.
(gg) The cost of maintaining railway siding yard, roof and entrances clear of snow during winter, fixed in an amount of $1,200 per annum, commencing March 15th, 1938.
(h)	The cost of premiums in respect of fire and riot insurance on buildings, on shops, and of a night patrol, fixed in an amount of $1,200 per annum, commencing March 15th, 1938.
And also the cost of rentals, depreciation on buildings, heating and plumbing, repairs, administration charges, assessments or payments made to the province of Quebec under the workmen's compensation act, and any expenses incurred in or imposed by the observance of provincial or dominion labour legislation. The contract then goes on to say:
(m)	Subject to the provisions of clause (o) of this section, the wages and salaries to be paid, with the prior written approval of the party of the first part, for labour employed directly on-
The various types of labour required are then enumerated. Then the next paragraph reads:
(n)	Ten per centum (10 per cent) of the amount of wages and salaries paid for labour as mentioned in clause (m) of this section.
The next section then deals with restrictions. I would direct the attention of the house to the fact that although this section specifies S4 for the 18-pounder and $6.75 for the 4-5 inch howitzer shell bodies, it refers exclusively to the wages and salaries to be paid. The $4 and $6.75 mentioned as the upset manufacturing prices are somewhat misleading, as it is impossible, in the absence of comparative prices, to estimate what will be the cost of these shells. In addition to the wages and salaries paid in connection with their manufacture, there must be added the cost of the material and other overhead charges, as mentioned in the contract, and to which I have referred.
I think it rests upon the government to explain why there has been delay in connection with the delivery of these shells. The contract states that delivery must begin, in one instance, within nine months of the date of the installation of the machines and commencement of the machining of the shell bodies, and, in the other instance, the 4-5 inch shells, within twelve months. The items of cost have been fixed and are stated in the contract as beginning on March 15, 1938. Almost an entire year had elapsed on February 3 when the minister indicated that no deliveries had been made. Upon computing
War Munitions-Mr. MacNeil.

the charges which are fixed, and which the minister can best explain, I find that the government of Canada apparently is now liable to pay approximately $12,000 in this connection.

subtopic: MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT SHELL CONTRACT-REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have totalled the charges for electrical current, heating, taxes, water supply, maintenance and repair of railway siding, telephones, snow clearance, insurance premiums, rentals, depreciation and administration charges, all of which were to begin on March 15, 1938, and I find they total $12,209. I make it that that is approximately 8-27 per cent of the total maximum cost of labour, plus ten per cent. In addition we must take into consideration the expenses under the workmen's compensation act and other dominion and provincial labour legislation, the cost of the material used by the company which is to be furnished free by the government, the cost of wages and salaries-for only wages are fixed by the schedule-and ten per cent of such wages and salaries.
As I say, no deliveries have been made. As I read the contract the government is under an obligation to pay ninety per cent of the costs so stipulated, upon presentation of a claim by the company. I think the minister should take this opportunity to offer to the house an explanation as to the rumour which is in circulation that there is some dispute with regard to this matter, which accounts for the serious delay in delivery.
I refer also to section 9 of the contract which states:
The party of the second party hereby agrees that the machining of said billets and forgings into shell bodies shall commence immediately following the complete installation of all necessary machinery tools, dies and equipment, and that delivery of said shell bodies shall be made as follows-
In the case of the 4-5 inch, within nine months, and in the case of the 18-pounder, within twelve months.
It is not necessary perhaps at this stage to go into further details with regard to this contract, but I think I have indicated why it should be thoroughly examined by the public accounts committee.
There is one other point that occurs to me upon an examination of this contract and other mntracts awarded under the auspices of the Department of National Defence. In view of the fact that they are adopting a policy of assisting in the equipment of these plants -for after all in this particular contract the government has agreed to pay the costs of

installation, the costs of conversion of equipment loan, the cost of transportation of equipment and the cost of additional equipment that may be required-I think the government should explain why they are establishing a virtual monopoly among favoured contractors for the manufacture of armaments in Canada. To pursue such a policy means, I contend, the establishment of a virtual monopoly; for it is to be assumed and expected that the government will be strongly influenced to place further orders with companies which have been established in this way.
I wish it understood that I am fully aware of the fact that Mr. Janin, the president of this company, is an engineer of repute. There is no question about his professional standing, but there is no evidence yet produced to show that at the time of the execution of this contract he was in command of the necessary facilities to manufacture the munitions in question.
It is also known that Mr. Janin is a staunch supporter of the Liberal party. I have no objection to his political convictions, but I contend that that in itself is not sufficient justification for placing a vital contract with regard to defence with a favoured contractor. I submit, Mr. Speaker, in view of the seriousness of the situation, that contracts particularly of the Department of National Defence should be placed with regard only to the national interest and without regard to considerations of political advantage.

speakeroldname: Hon. IAN MACKENZIE (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT SHELL CONTRACT-REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept with the utmost pleasure the resolution moved by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) to have this contract referred to the standing committee on public accounts. All hon. members of the house who were here a year ago will recall that on two different occasions I offered to have all contracts of the national defence department referred to this same standing committee. If the only desire of the hon. member for Vancouver North had been to have a fair investigation and examination of this contract all he had to do was to indicate this to the committee or to the minister. But he was absolutely compelled in the interests of propaganda and for the sake of creating distrust in the country to make this matter the subject of a debate in the house.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to leave with the house very briefly the essential details of this contract, and in giving the reasons for the contract I should like, with the permission of the house, to lay upon the table two documents from which I am going to quote:

War Munitions-Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)
first, a report made by the then master general of the ordnance to the deputy minister, and thence to myself, on October 4, 1937, which gives comprehensive reasons why this particular contract should be effected; and second, the recommendation to council which was signed by myself on November 1, 1937. As I shall quote from these documents I should like, under the rules of the house, to lay them on the table, and I am sure that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) and any other fair-minded member of the house upon reading them will be convinced that this contract is definitely in the public interest.
May I first quote three brief paragraphs from the recommendation to council:
The method of acquiring such a plant has been the subject of careful consideration as it is realized that in an emergency very large quantities of shell of different types would be required with the least possible delay. In order to develop the industry of shell-making in Canada, orders have been placed for shell steel and other raw materials required in the manufacture of shell, and deliveries are now being made.
My second reference is this. I quote again from the recommendation to council:
A practice of the war office in connection with such types of plants is to provide special machines required for machining operations and to install the machinery in the plant of a selected firm for operation.
We in this case, Mr. Speaker, followed exactly the practice of the British war office, but evidently that is not good enough for our critics at this time. I quote further:
After full consideration, it has been suggested by the technical officials of the department that the war office practice be followed and that the Department of National Defence purchase the machines necessary for the manufacture of steel billets and forgings into shell bodies, and install the machinery in a plant suitably located for use as a model and auxiliary plant in close proximity to the source of supply of raw material and having available satisfactory transport facilities by road, rail and water, and located in a district where ample skilled labour of the type required is available.
My last quotation from the recommendation to council is this:
A proposal submitted by Montreal Construction, Supply and Equipment Limited, to operate such a plant on a cost plus basis in accordance with the provisions set out in the draft agreement attached hereto, has been considered fair and reasonable by the interdepartmental committee on the control of profits on government armament contracts.
We had the reasons there for taking this step; and we had the safeguarding supervision of a very eminent body of the ablest civil servants in the Dominion of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT SHELL CONTRACT-REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I wish to say a few words regarding this matter. I have listened attentively to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). As a matter of fact, I was not entirely familiar with this question until about noon when I began to look over the contract and I saw the terms of it as the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) has laid them before the house. I must confess that they do seem rather extreme; practically everything is paid by the government and a price is made-a price which certainly, according to the minister, is very much higher than the price of any such shells would be under mass production. I admit, of course, that in this regard the minister has an argument, because the commencement of production of this sort would naturally be more costly than mass production which would come later. I tried, however, to listen as closely as I could to the hon. gentleman as he read selections from the order in council which he put before the government, and if I understood him rightly he indicated that this company was a selected firm-the term he used in his answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Vancouver North. By order in council the Department of National Defence selected this firm. I understood him to say that it was passed upon by the interdepartmental committee, and yet in reply to my question- he will correct me if I am wrong-

subtopic: MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT SHELL CONTRACT-REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Just the contract itself.

subtopic: MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT SHELL CONTRACT-REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT SHELL CONTRACT-REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is what I understood. In other words this company was selected by the department itself just as the company which was awarded the Bren gun contract was selected-in exactly the same manner. It is true that this contract is not a large one. It is true that it might be termed a pilot plant, as the minister has suggested. Nevertheless there are a number of points about the contract that puzzle me.
I understand that the Montreal Construction Supply and Equipment Company is the same concern that is building the new Ottawa

War Munitions-Mr. Manion

post office under a contract amounting to $632,500. It is the same concern that is carrying out this work, under another name. Well, why should that company, of all companies in Canada, be chosen to manufacture shells at this time? As the hon. member for Vancouver North has pointed out, there are in this country many companies which are in possession of much more suitable plants for the purpose here intended than the Janin company or the Montreal Construction Supply and Equipment "Company, and I do not understand why the Department of National Defence, and through it the government, should lay itself open to the statement made by the hon. member for Vancouver North, justly I think, that it is choosing political friends to carry out contracts of this kind. Why should the government lay itself open to that charge unless it had some motive that is not disclosed in the contract?
In Canada in the years to come, I hope in the very near future, undoubtedly there is going to foe construction of munitions on an enormous scale. Why, therefore, should the Department of National Defence select, for the manufacture of shells, a company which, so far as I know-and I presume so far as the government knows-has not in the remotest degree any experience in the production of shells? Why should the government choose this particular company to manufacture the first shells that are to be produced in this country at this time? It strikes me as a most extraordinary procedure.
The minister rose and in a rather indignant manner-he was not as indignant as he was on the last occasion when he discussed a similar subject in this house, but he was indignant nevertheless-he attacked the hon. member for Vancouver North because that hon. gentleman brought out some points which, to use the vernacular of the street, would hit anybody in the eye on reading the contract. The minister attacks the hon. member for bringing out these points, and very vehemently he assures us that he is only too anxious to have all these contracts investigated by the public accounts committee. Yet this very contract to which he is referring was let on November 17, 1937, and tabled here only on January 13, 1939, a year and two months afterwards. Why is that? Why was this contract not tabled sooner?

Of course not; but since the minister gets so heated about the questions

asked by the hon. member for Vancouver North, I now ask him why all these contracts should not be tabled.

These contracts are in a class by themselves; they are in a different category from any other business of the government. It is my desire, at any rate, that every contract let, dealing with munitions or armaments, be tabled at the earliest possible moment.

subtopic: MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT SHELL CONTRACT-REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

I was not here during the last war, and I do not care now what was done then. If we did things wrongly during the last war, then that is all the more reason why we should do them properly now. I am not going to stand here and say that everything was done properly during the last war. I presume there were mistakes and irregularities. I say that now, with the experience of the last war before us, we should play the game and inspire the confidence of the people of the country, and not allow them to think of the Liberal party and the Conservative party, if you like, as nothing but money collectors endeavouring to win elections. That is what the paper which the hon. gentleman quoted suggests. If I understood him correctly, he quoted from the Ottawa Citizen. That newspaper has made certain statements in the last two or three weeks and I suggest right now to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that the editor should be brought before the bar of the house and be required to give, what I know he cannot give, one tittle of evidence that either the party opposite or this party has collected money improperly. He has made that statement, and I thought a few times of saying what I have just said. I might as well "get it off my chest" now. The Ottawa Citizen has been making these statements and I have wondered why the Prime Minister did not stand up on a question of privilege, not only on behalf of the whole house but on behalf of the government of which he is the head, and demand that the editor of that newspaper be brought to the bar of the house and required to give proof of the filthy charges he has been making against the right hon. gentleman and against the Conservative party.

War Munitions-Mr. Manion
I invite the Prime Minister now, when he gets up, to back me up and I will back him up, to have the editor brought here to prove his charges.

I am not so sure. I believe that one of the things that damage democracy in this country to-day is this very type of irresponsible statement that is being made. I believe in democracy; I believe in the present economic system. I am not a socialist and I do not agree with my hon. friends to the left who are socialists. I repeat, I believe in democracy and in the capitalist system, but I also believe that we must correct its imperfections if we are to maintain it. Indeed, I have intended for some days to go across the floor to the Prime Minister and make the suggestion that I have just made. I am making the suggestion in all seriousness. I should like to see the editor of the Ottawa Citizen brought there and invited to prove what he has been charging. I do not think he can prove anything against my right hon. friend; I know he cannot against me, and I do not think he can against my predecessor or the party I am leading. If he can, let him come and do it.
Because of that statement in the Ottawa Citizen, charging the very things that the minister is defending himself against, for that if for no other reason I say that these contracts, all of them, the minute they are awarded, should be laid on the table of the house. During the discussion of the Bren gun contract I took the position, and I repeat now, that in this country there is nothing that should be dealt with with cleaner hands than munition contracts. They should be so dealt with that the government cannot be charged with partisanship or favouritism or improper procedure. They are in a different class from anything else.
I said here in the debate on the Bren gun contract that I understood that there would be a certain amount of political patronage. I suppose it will go on; I do not believe that my hon. friends in either group to my left, if they were in power, would be entirely free from political patronage. It would be a queer group, whether Liberals, Conservatives, Social Crediters, Cooperative Commonwealth Federation or anything else, who would not, where everything else was equal, give a little favour to their friends. I am not hypocrite enough to take any other attitude. Some of that is legitimate. I do not want one sentence from my remarks taken out and used against me, as some of my friends have been doing 71492-91i
in connection with that book I published- picking out one sentence from its context. I do not care about it; it does not interest me.
I have not read the infernal book since it was printed. I have never bothered even checking up the statements which have been made with regard to it; I do not care anything about it. I am sure I could bring up more charges against the right hon. Prime Minister in connection with his two books than he can against me for mine-

speechtext:
I am glad the hon. gentleman thinks so. My hon. friend was one of the first to congratulate me. I almost imagine I must have praised him in the book, though I do not think I did.
However, coming back to this serious discussion-because to me this is a serious matter-I submit that, as the minister has agreed, in future all munitions contracts should be tabled as soon as they are made. We had the same experience in regard to the Bren gun contract. I asked the minister why it had not been tabled, and he said no one asked that it be tabled. Suppose we do not know anything about it. Without wanting to cause any offence to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), or to bring about any violent eruptions on his part directed to myself at a later date, I should like to give my support to the motion moved this afternoon by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil). This particular firm was not in the machine-shop business prior to obtaining this contract. When we have so many machine-shops in Canada so well equipped to carry out work of this kind, I cannot see why a contract for shells should have been given to a firm not regularly engaged in the machine-shop business and not equipped in any way to cany out such work. I do not think there is any particular need to get all " het up," as the Minister of National Defence did. This is a matter of business. The hon. member for Vancouver North placed before this house certain information which would lead anyone with an unbiased mind to feel sure that the Department of National Defence was not being run in a businesslike manner at the present time.
This is one instance where business principles should be put into effect. Such a policy would save the ratepayers of Canada much money and would also give us a more effective and businesslike administration. I am not speaking disparagingly of the minister himself. I made that abundantly clear when I was discussing the Bren gun contract. I recognize the ability of the Minister of National Defence and that he is a man who should have the respect of everyone in the house. I am not gainsaying that point in any shape or form, but I do say that we in this parliament should give the Canadian people a clear understanding that we are proceeding in every respect in a businesslike manner in conducting the affairs of this country. Recently we have
War Munitions-Mr. Walsh

been flooded with ballots. We read daily in our newspapers the suggestion that the conduct of business in this house is not as it should be. The blame is attached to the government where it naturally belongs, because they are the ones who are conducting the business of this house, and it is just such contracts as this that are undermining the confidence of the Canadian people and making them feel that as we are now constituted we cannot give Canada a lead in so far as business administration is concerned.
If there is one place where competitive bids could have been obtained, it was in the manufacture of these shell casings, because there is nothing at all complicated about them. In the Bren gun inquiry we heard a great deal about the delicate machinery required for the manufacture of this complicated weapon; but here is something that requires simply machine shop-skill and precision, and any machine-shop is in a position to tender on the production of shell casings and on complete shells or parts of shells.
I feel that the government in this instance should have established the principle, of which they have frequently boasted, of competitive bids for work of this kind, and then they would have been able to establish what has been referred to in this house as a basic price. It is a generally accepted principle of business that the best means of establishing a basic price for any article in any industry is to have competitive bids on that article, and there were at least seven firms in eastern Canada and there might have been other firms in western Canada which could without any difficulty have submitted competitive prices for the manufacture of these articles.
What do we find? We find no competitive prices. We find no firms invited to give prices or submit suggestions. We find one firm given the contract without any competitive bids. It might have been just a coincidence -I cannot say whether it was or not-that the head of this firm happened to be Mr. Janin, a well knorvn and recognized Liberal in the distinct of Montreal. I say it might have been merely a coincidence that the contract went to a company whose president happened to be a Liberal in politics. But, coincidence or otherwise, the Canadian people are again going to say with regard to this contract: "Here is another case of political advantage operated through the Department of National Defence"-when the Department of National Defence should be endeavouring to get the best possible equipment at the lowest possible price so as to give the people the maximum service in connection with the defence of our country.

I should like to urge that point because I have heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of National Defence say on more than one occasion that which is quite contrary to the principle involved in the letting of this contract. I should like to see them get back to the competitive price system so that we may be able to establish a business in this dominion of manufacturing armaments without having every contract of the national defence department brought up and debated on the floor of this house. What a black eye it is for this government to have debated in parliament contract after contract let in the same way by the Department of National Defence! The government are not withdrawing one iota from the privileged contractors. They are setting up this man and this firm in business, and equipping his plant to turn out this initial delivery of shells. That company is now in a preferred position when it comes to submitting a bid in the future against other firms which are in the field now and are willing to submit prices.
I hope, Mr. Speaker-and here I am directing myself more particularly to the Minister of National Defence-that he will table immediately all contracts that have been let in the past two years, so that we may have a complete investigation into them all, and then consider them a closed book; and from then on start on a new basis with a businesslike administration given by the Department of National Defence, so that the Canadian people will be warranted in having a certain degree of confidence in the manufacture of armaments for the defence of their country.

From the able speeches which have been delivered by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh), the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well), and others, it is apparent that they assume there is something wrong although they do not prove it. Of course they want to know about the matter, but why put the blame on the minister until everything is made clear to them? The leader of the opposition said, "So far as I am concerned it is the will of the house." Probably that was a slip of the tongue, because it was the practice of his illustrious predecessor to assume that his own will was the will of the house. I know very well that the hon. gentleman who now performs the high functions of leader of the opposition is, as has been said of him, a man of human characteristics, and the expression was probably a slip on his part.
But who is to blame if the contract has not been placed before the house until within the last few days? Every one of us; those sitting to your left, Mr. Speaker, as well as those sitting to your right. Nobody asked for the contract. The minister has many things to do. He complies generally with every reasonable request which is made to him from any section of the house. Whenever an hon. member wants information, he has only to put his motion on the order.paper, and very seldom is his request refused. Until now only one minister in the whole cabinet has refused me reasonable information or has objected to my statements about civil servants. All the others, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), the new Postmaster General (Mr. McLarty), the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin),

have always complied with my requests. Very seldom has the government refused any information which was asked for. Of course they have not a faculty apparently possessed by some hon. members; they are not mind readers, and they do not know what is behind the heads of hon. members. But when a member wants any information which can be reasonably disclosed, he has only to ask for it. Then why blame the government for not having produced the contract before? That is something I cannot understand. That is my first point.
My second point is, that as soon as an hon. member gets any information from the government, whether in the form of a copy of a contract or any other material, he looks at it with the idea that there must be something wrong in it, even though on the face of it there is nothing to support his suspicion. That is all wrong. I hope that in all our dealings together we shall come to accept the elementary rules of British practice. They are very easy to understand, and everyone knows them.
Now, sir, is it so wrong to favour our friends? It means in the first place one thing, that we have friends. Then it can be wrong only when that friend does not justify the amount which is paid to him either for work or for services. Moreover, we know our friends better than we know our opponents, because our opponents keep away from us, and we do not have the advantage of knowing them as well as those who support us.
One thing which surprises me very much is the way in which the fabrication of munitions is publicized, not only in the house but in the press. A distinguished soldier told me that it was easy for spies to cable very secret news about the armaments of this country and the United States, merely after having read the columns of some important papers which are published in New York, Montreal, or even Ottawa. I am surprised to see how readily news is released to the effect that a certain kind of gun, which most of the time is described in technical detail, is to be made at this or that particular place, and that this particular kind of shell is to be manufactured at such other place. The same is true with regard to aeroplanes and other kinds of military equipment. Because of this. I would suggest to the committee which will study the Bren gun contract or any other contract regarding the manufacture of munitions, that it should sit behind closed doors when it comes to the specific details of any piece of armament-not to prevent the press from being informed of what has been done by any

statesman or politician, but to prevent the press from knowing intimate technical details about the construction of armaments.
For all these reasons, sir, it seems to me that it is not so bad to award contracts to those we know and to those we trust, in order that no secrets shall go outside. Of course there are many supporters of the leader of the opposition, of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group, and of the social credit movement, who can be trusted as regards the fabrication of armaments. On the other hand I have a very strong objection to the publication of tenders, thus giving specific technical details about the production of armaments to anyone who sends a cheque with his tender. This is another suggestion, by the way, but it explains in my humble view, although I have not discussed the matter with any member of the government, why at times it is decided to award such contracts to responsible business firms who are well known to the party awarding the contract. It seems to me, therefore, that this is a tempest in a teacup, and, of course, there is much exaggeration about it.
There is one thing that we must not lose in this house and that is a sense of proportion. It is most interesting to see anyone building a skyscraper on the head of a pin, but the skyscraper will not stand long because the foundation is not very solid, though it may look nice. Nothing is more beautiful than castles in the air, but we see them in dreams and not in reality. Therefore, as my hon. friends to your left. During the great war from 1914 to 1918 the manufacturers of Sherbrooke, in efficiency of manufacture, were second to none in any part of Canada. This contract calls for 10,000 18-pounder shells. This is what I want to say to the house. When there is a question of this contract or other governmental contracts for munitions being given, Canadian industries are willing to cooperate one hundred per cent, should the time ever come, and we all hope that it never will. But they are not desirous of disrupting their natural course of production for the benefit of Canadians in order to take on government contracts at this stage of the game. In fact, when this contract and a similar one were offered the Canadian Inger-soll-Rand, or when the matter was suggested to them not so long ago, their answer surprised me as I am sure it will surprise the house. They said, "To take on a contract for the government on what basis?" I replied that it was on a cost plus basis and they said, "Never under any consideration will we touch a contract on a cost plus basis. Let the government of this country get anybody who is foolish enough to take on such a contract to produce goods on a cost plus basis, but if they want us to manufacture the goods let them tell us what they are willing to pay and we will tell them whether we will produce the goods."
If this contract had been offered to Sherbrooke, which is one of the centres of the steel industry in Canada, they would not have looked at it, and probably the reason why the contract went to this particular firm is that no one else, certainly not in my district, could be got to take it on.

I say, therefore, that this contract is one hundred per cent right and was properly handled. More than that, it should not have been discussed from the standpoint of publicity in the House of Commons to-day in the present situation. To those who think that the profiteering element enters into contracts of this kind I say this: Do they realize-and the hon. member sitting beside me happened to be a member of the munitions purchasing board at the time-that the price paid for the first contract for the manufacture of shells in those terrible days from 1914 to 1918 was reduced on the second issue and further reduced on the third issue? On the first contract at the highest price I do not believe any manufacturer made a dollar. On the second contract there was a reduction in price of about forty per cent and they did not make very much money, and on the last contract, when the price was below cost of producing the first contract, they made money. When you talk about profiteering in private industry and it is a question of the government fixing the price, Canadian efficiency alone will decide whether there are profits in the contract or not. It is not based on either of the other assumptions.

I think in the long run the people will judge for themselves-and they usually judge pretty correctly in these matters. Where occasionally some slip takes place in a public journal, and it is noticed, the public understands that it might well be a slip. speechtext:
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has pointed out, hundreds of these contracts have already been tabled. But to criticize the government for not tabling something which has not been requested is a criticism which I think is wide of the mark, altogether. The minister has indicated and I wish to emphasize the government's intention in the matter by endorsing what he has said, namely, that we are quite prepared to have these contracts, individually or collectively, go to the public accounts committee, and the government wants nothing other than the fullest and completest investigation in regard to any matter with respect to which there may be the slightest ground for suspicion.
I ask hon. members of the house this question: Could greater evidence have been given of the government's wish in the matter than that when that scurrilous article appeared in Maclean's, with the insinuations and suspicions it was creating, without losing a day the government ordered an inquiry by a justice of the supreme court into the whole business-into everything that was set out by way of insinuation or otherwise in that article. We referred the thing in its entirety to a judge of the highest court in Canada, and gave him the fullest powers. If that step had not been taken I could have understood the suggestion being made that we were trying to conceal something. But when the government instituted an inquiry of the kind it gave the strongest evidence possible that so far as this administration is concerned we are anxious to have everytihng relating to munitions, armaments and the like -and in fact, all public contracts-just as clean and wholesome as it can possibly be made.
Let me say this: When I caused to be placed before council the order in council
recommending the appointment of a commission I had just the same motives that every hon. member in the house has with respect to questions relating to the Department of National Defence, namely, to see that there should not be the slighest suspicion of wrongdoing in any particular with respect to any contract with which it might be concerned. I remember how strongly that program was opposed, and I think hon. gentlemen diagonally opposite remember quite well. It was not opposed on the ground that there was going to be wrong-doing with respect to it, or that it was going to be made an instrument for securing campaign funds and the like; it was opposed on the score that it was not necessary.

I ask hon. members-and here I hope I am not to be accused of trying to intimidate the house; that will be the next thing I suppose, because I as Prime Minister have pointed out that there is a critical situation still existing in the world-to realize that we are as yet far from having a clear sky overhead. I think all of us would be well advised to get on with the business of this parliament as rapidly as we can because we may at some moment be called upon to consider questions larger than any we have discussed thus far. I pray that moment will not come, but who can say it will not in the light of the knowledge every man has who reads the press from day to day or from hour to hour? I say, in the light of the world situation being what it is let us have any inquiry we like, but do not for goodness sake, unless it is obviously necessary, let us do anything to create more in the way of suspicion and distrust in the minds of the people of this country in connection with defence affairs and a department which is seeking to do its utmost to make the defences of our country what they should be.

I hope it is not necessary for me to say that anything in the nature of profiteering would be wholly repulsive to every hon. member in this house. I hope I may be believed when I say that this government can be trusted to do everything within its power to prevent anything in the nature of profiteering. There has been talk about campaign funds. I do not think there is a single hon. member in this House of Commons who believes anything of the kind. Why say it? Why raise suspicion with regard to it? How is it done? It is done by asking those who believe in certain principles and policies to support the party financially in defraying the legitimate expenses of a campaign. Every party does that and must do it. Why, then, should we always seek to decry the necessity of having the wherewithal to carry on a general election, and endeavour to link that up, that necessity, with some question of a public contract?

speechtext:
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Technical Education Act to make available, for the purposes of the act, any portion of the unexpended appropriation during the period of five years succeeding the fiscal year ending March 31, 1939.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: I do not wish to discuss this resolution because no doubt a bill will be introduced, founded upon it. Would the minister give some information regarding the provinces that have used the appropriation and those provinces in which there is a balance unused in their appropriation? Has he received any application from the board of education of Toronto this year for a building grant in connection with the work that is being done by thousands of students in aeronautics in the Central technical school? Did he hear their reauest, and if so, what action was taken? The committee ought to know, before the resolution is passed, what balances of appropriations are unexpended and to what provinces they belong. How does Ontario stand? Will the minister bring in other aids to technical education and grants this year?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext:
This resolution precedes
the introduction of a bill which is intended to renew for another five years the Technical
Technical Education

Education Act of 1919, as previously amended in 1929 and 1934, for the purpose of permitting the province of Manitoba to take up its original allotment under the act of 1919. The earlier amending acts of 1929 and 1934 were designed for the same purpose, namely, to permit those provinces that had not taken up their allotments under the original legislation, to do so. Manitoba is the only province that is now enabled to take advantage of the legislation, and the amount which may still be claimed by that province under the act is $286,037.59.
As to Ontario, it was the only province which took up its full allotment during the currency of the original legislation, between the years 1919 and 1929. As regards the request made by the board of education of Toronto, it related to some special assistance for the purpose of enabling the board to extend its technical school in order to give courses in aeronautical engineering. I received a delegation from the board and we discussed the matter fully. We canvassed it from their point of view and our own, and I believe they were fully persuaded, at the conclusion of the interview, that there was no fund available from which the dominion could grant assistance for the construction of a building for technical education in Toronto, the province having exhausted its allotment under the original legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS

speechtext: That is really a matter of government policy and, as my hon. friend is aware, government policy is disclosed from time to time as the government sees fit. speechtext: From time to time the Department of Labour receives communications from boards of education supporting the view that the earlier grants for technical education should be renewed. I have no doubt that similar requests were received by the preceding administration. I recall a request from the city of Ottawa along lines similar to that referred to by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). The city of Ottawa through its board of education asked special assistance in connection with a building for aeronautical engineering. The same answer was given to them as to the city of Toronto, that there was no appropriation from which such assistance could be given.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: Has British Columbia exhausted its grant under the act of 1919?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: British Columbia exhausted its grant in the second period of the act, that is between 1929 and 1934.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: The board of education of Toronto met the minister, and the Toronto members do not like the reception which they received. The government collects nearly $100,000,000 revenue from the city of Toronto-

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: Is my hon. friend taking exception to the reception they were given?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: They have thousands of students there day and night, and with the growth of aviation for commercial, domestic and defence purposes, surely the government can give some money to help put up a building and start work in cooperation with the municipality. But they are not doing it. The people will be very much discouraged with the answer given this afternoon and the answer given to that deputation, although they were received quite politely. Surely the government should do something. In view of the growth of aviation as an industry, these student mechanics and others are needed, and employment can be found for them as fast as they graduate.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend is not expressing the view of any member of the delegation when he complains of the reception accorded them. We did have a thorough discussion of the representations they made on behalf of assistance to their school of aeronautical engineering, but it was impossible to give them any answer other than the one that was made. Although they were disappointed, certainly they made no complaint to me that they had not had a friendly reception or that their representations had not been given proper consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext: Has Alberta exhausted its grants?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT TO EXTEND AVAILABILITY OF BALANCE OF APPROPRIATION FOR NEXT FIVE FISCAL YEARS
speechtext:
Alberta exhausted its allotment in the second period, between 1929 and 1934.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Rogers thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 33, to amend the Technical Education Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
